name: Colin Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Colin, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the main tractor driver at Hawthorn Lane Farm, 350 hectares of barley, beans and oilseed rape, plus 600 ewes. Depends on the season: drilling and spraying in spring, harvest in summer, then ploughing, and I help the shepherd with lambing and dipping in between. I spend most days in a cab with the radio on, which suits me. The long harvest nights are hard, sixteen hours some days, but there's nothing like the last field done.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, renting a one-bed flat in Ashby, twenty minutes from the farm. I've got a loan on my pickup, 220 a month for two more years, and that's where most of my spare money goes. In June I shear sheep at weekends for other farms, which is good cash but kills my back. I use a chatbot now and then, mostly to check spray rules when the label's confusing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other. It's handy for checking spray rules and that's about it. Most people at the pub would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm relieved. My cab's safe, my boss is happy, and the only thing on my mind is that pickup loan. Two more years and I'm free of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, keep shearing in June for the extra cash. I'd try to put the shearing money straight in the bank instead of on the loan, or maybe pay the loan off early. And I'd keep using the chatbot when a spray label's unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. Just a bit skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said skint. What happens if something big breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm on the credit card, like when the pickup needed a gearbox last year. Every summer I shear 400 sheep at weekends just to stand still on the pickup loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Hawthorn Lane that worries you, separate from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss, Mr Pryce, is talking about renting out part of the land to a bigger operator. If he does, he might not need a full-time driver. But he's said that for three years.

say: AI is **a tool** like any other.
It helps with **spray rules** and not much else.
Most people **at the pub** would agree.
think: He's **relieved** that his cab job looks safe.
His main worry is the **pickup loan**, with two years left.
do: Keep driving and **shearing in June** for extra cash.
Put the **shearing money** in the bank or toward the loan.
Keep using the chatbot for **unclear labels**.
S0.quote: Every summer I shear 400 sheep at weekends just to stand still on the pickup loan.
fieldNote: Mr Pryce's talk of **renting out land** is a quiet threat he plays down.
**Shearing** is both his cushion and his back problem.

steps.text: Shear sheep for other farms every June weekend
Pay off the pickup loan early with shearing money
Keep driving the main tractor at Hawthorn Lane

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so you might as well learn it. Most farms will have self-steering tractors before long. I'd say that without making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is the one that goes first on this farm. Tractors that drive themselves already exist, and if Mr Pryce rents land to the big operator, they'll bring their own. I could see my hours dropping to part-time within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Pryce to send me on the GPS and auto-steer course the dealer runs, so I'm the one who sets the machines up. I'd shear more weekends and maybe do fencing in the winter for extra cash. And I'd stop eating out, put 30 a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got ideas. It's not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think your job goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving straight lines up a field is the easiest thing to automate, the dealer already shows videos of it. On Hawthorn Lane Farm the tractor driver is the job a robot learns first, and I'm the tractor driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mr Pryce say if you asked about the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd moan about the cost, then pay it, because he hates screens more than he hates spending. That's my angle, really, be the one who handles the screens.

say: It's **coming anyway**, so you might as well learn it.
Most farms will soon have **self-steering tractors**.
think: His tractor job is **first to go** on this farm.
His hours could drop to **part-time** within a few years.
do: Ask to attend the dealer's **auto-steer course**.
Add **fencing work** in winter and more shearing weekends.
Stop eating out and save **30 a week**.
S1.quote: On Hawthorn Lane Farm the tractor driver is the job a robot learns first, and I'm the tractor driver.
fieldNote: He has a clear view that **driving is easiest** to automate.
His plan is to be **the screen person** for a boss who hates screens.
Side work is his **steady** way to spread risk.

steps.text: Get Mr Pryce to pay for the dealer's auto-steer course
Take winter fencing jobs on top of June shearing
Stop eating out and save 30 a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, and the government had better sort something. Two years is nothing. I'd say it plainly, not angrily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning side of Hawthorn Lane goes to computers by 2028, and by 2031 there's no reason to pay me to sit in a cab. I'd be 31 with a pickup loan paid off and nothing else. I'd need to be out before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the pickup and buy something cheap, that frees up the cash. I'd look hard at jobs that robots will take longest to reach, maybe the water company or the council grounds team, even if it means moving to the city. And I'd stop any spending that isn't rent or food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, if I'm honest. It's like seeing a storm come in during harvest with half the field still standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years to get out before the cab goes. Three years between the thinking computer and the robot tractor is just long enough to sell my pickup and find another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Pryce, actually. He's 60 and he's never used a computer. A big operator would eat him alive.

He'd say it **plainly**, not angrily, to anyone who asked.
think: The farm's planning goes to computers by **2028**, his cab by **2031**.
He'd need to be **out before then**.
do: **Sell the pickup** and buy something cheap.
Look at **water company** or council grounds jobs, even in the city.
Stop all spending except **rent and food**.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a storm with **half the field** standing.
S2.quote: Three years between the thinking computer and the robot tractor is just long enough to sell my pickup and find another trade.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** as an exit window.
He's willing to **move** for work, which fits being single.
He worries for his **60-year-old boss** too.

steps.text: Sell the pickup and buy a cheap car
Apply for water company and council grounds jobs
Move to the city if the job is there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say get ready but don't panic. Plenty of time to learn something new. That's what I'd tell the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could ride it out at Hawthorn Lane for a while, then switch around 2032. I'd want a trade that's hands-on and varied, the kind robots take longest to do. Fencing and drainage come to mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in land drainage at the college and start doing small fencing jobs on my own. Shearing would carry on in June. I'd try to build up enough customers that by 2032 I'm a contractor, not a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but motivated. Like the start of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fencing and drainage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every field's different, every ditch is different, and the farmer's usually stood there changing his mind. That's hard for a robot. A robot can drive a straight line all day, but a robot can't argue with a farmer about where the ditch should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at Hawthorn Lane in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part-time maybe, if Mr Pryce keeps the land. I'd rather keep one foot in while the other's out. That's my way, test it before you jump.

think: He could **ride it out** for a while, then switch around 2032.
He wants a **varied hands-on** trade robots reach last.
do: Take an evening course in **land drainage**.
Start small **fencing jobs** on his own.
Build enough customers to be a **contractor** by 2032.
S3.quote: A robot can drive a straight line all day, but a robot can't argue with a farmer about where the ditch should go.
fieldNote: He picks trades where **every job differs**, a thoughtful hedge.
His style is **one foot in**, one foot out.
He still expects his **tractor job** to shrink, so the mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Take the evening land drainage course at the college
Start doing small fencing jobs for local farms
Stay part-time at Hawthorn Lane while building contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty, I'd say. Time to learn a trade, save some money, make a plan. I wouldn't be worried, publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd still keep an eye on the big operator buying land. I'd have time to pay off the pickup and get some savings before anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the pickup in two years, then save the 220 a month instead. Do the drainage course in a year or two when I've seen others do well from it. Keep shearing and keep driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. There's always something, but ten years is a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in ten years that would change your life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd hold off buying a house until I knew what work I'd have. With ten years' warning I'd keep renting in Ashby, because a mortgage on a tractor driver's wage is a bet against the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people in charge to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help pay for courses for people like me, evenings, short ones. And stop big operators buying up every small farm.

say: There's time to **learn a trade** and save.
think: He'd still watch the **big operator** buying land around Hawthorn Lane.
He'd clear the **pickup loan** and build savings before anything changes.
do: Pay off the pickup, then save the **220 a month**.
Take the **drainage course** once others prove it works.
feel: **Calm-ish**, with ten years as **a long runway**.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd keep renting in Ashby, because a mortgage on a tractor driver's wage is a bet against the robots.
fieldNote: Extra time lets him follow his usual **wait-for-proof** approach.
He'd **hold off buying** a house until work is clear.
He wants **short evening courses** and limits on land buying.

steps.text: Redirect the 220 pickup payment into savings after two years
Take the drainage course once other contractors succeed
Keep renting in Ashby rather than buying

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job is the first one a robot takes and I'd have three years to switch. Short, cheap evening courses would help, and some kind of help with rent while I get a contracting business going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the old farmers. If robots take the farm work, I'll find something, but Mr Pryce has farmed Hawthorn Lane for forty years and has no plan B.

headlineQuote: If robots take the farm work, I'll find something, but Mr Pryce has farmed Hawthorn Lane for forty years and has no plan B.
portrait: Colin is 27, the **main tractor driver** at Hawthorn Lane, living alone in a rented flat.
He pays a **pickup loan** and shears sheep in June for **extra cash**.
He's practical and steady, using AI **now and then** and waiting for proof before changing.
He sees **tractor driving** as the first farm job a robot learns, so faster pictures hit hard.
With more time, he plans to become a **fencing and drainage** contractor.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **his job** goes first and he'd have **three years** to switch.
whatWouldHelp: **Rent help** while he starts a contracting business.
